The Agile wallaby (Macropus agilis) exhibits a maximum reproductive output that approaches one joey per year [Ri = one joey per year], a modest rate that appears to be constrained by the energetic demands of prolonged lactation in tropical savanna environments. Captive studies maintaining individuals at a mean core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] indicate that females rarely produce more than a single joey annually, reflecting the species' reliance on consistent forage availability to sustain pregnancy and the extensive nursing period that follows. Neonates emerge after an exceptionally brief gestation lasting approximately 29.4 days [tg = approximately 29.4 days], a remarkably short duration even among macropodids, and weigh merely 0.634 grams [Wwb = 0.634 grams] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] at birth. This minuscule birth mass, among the smallest relative to maternal size in the mammal lineage, underscores the fundamentally altricial state of the newborn joey, which must complete most of its morphological development within the maternal pouch under the stable thermal conditions provided by the dam.

Following parturition, the neonatal joey undergoes a prolonged period of dependent development within the pouch, relying entirely on milk for its nutritional requirements. A detailed growth trajectory compiled from captive reared individuals, recorded at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], reveals rapid mass gain from approximately 63 grams at six days of age to 600 grams by 34 days, and further to 4205 grams by 159 days post-partum. This accelerated growth phase is fueled by maternal milk production, which averages approximately 91178.08 joules per day  across the annual cycle, a substantial energetic investment that supports the joey's transition from a tiny altricial newborn to a sizeable pouch young at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The steady increase continues, with animals reaching about 9400 grams by 249 days, approaching the early juvenile mass range as the time for nutritional independence draws near.

The weaning process in Macropus agilis represents a critical developmental transition, culminating in full nutritional independence from the mother. Field observations and captive colony records converge on a weaning age of approximately 328 days since birth [tx = approximately 328 days since birth], at which point the young wallaby attains a wet body mass averaging 2287 grams [Wwx = 2287 grams] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This mass at weaning is consistent with the lower range of values documented for other medium-sized macropodids, reflecting the species' relatively rapid progression to independent foraging in its seasonally productive riparian habitats. The cessation of suckling marks the end of the mother's considerable lactational investment, which, at a maintenance temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], represents a daily energy expenditure that is a significant component of the female's overall reproductive budget and contributes to the observed interval between successive breeding events.

Sexual maturation in the Agile wallaby follows a protracted developmental schedule relative to many eutherian mammals of comparable adult size. Puberty, defined by the onset of reproductive capability, is reached at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth], a milestone that coincides with the attainment of a wet body mass of approximately 3510 grams [Wwp = approximately 3510 grams] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This body mass at puberty represents roughly 22 percent of the ultimate adult mass, suggesting that a threshold somatic size must be achieved before reproductive activation can proceed. The timing of maturation, occurring at an average core temperature regime of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], is closely tied to the species' seasonal breeding schedule, as females typically come into their first oestrus during periods of peak forage quality following the monsoon rains, ensuring that the energetic demands of gestation and early lactation coincide with resource abundance.

Adult Agile wallabies ultimately reach an asymptotic body mass of up to 16000 grams [Wwi = up to 16000 grams], a figure that represents the maximum recorded wet weight among wild populations and aligns with the upper bound of the species typically cited range of 10 to 15 kilograms. Field surveys and captive longevity records indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 16.9 years, converted to roughly 6169 days [am = roughly 6169 days] under the stable metabolic conditions of a 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] thermal environment. This lifespan is relatively extended for a macropodid of this body size and appears to be linked to the species' low adult mortality risk in its productive floodplain habitats, where dense vegetation offers cover from predators. The combination of a low annual reproductive rate, extended lactation, and delayed maturation underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival and adult persistence over high fecundity in the variable yet resource-rich Australian wet-dry tropics.
